prompt.context: Marie's Café is a small local coffee shop that serves coffee and latte. Marie's has been around for decades and is known for its high quality drinks and cozy atmosphere. The café has seen declining profits over the last few quarters, and the owner has hired you to increase its profits.
prompt.question: How would you help Marie's Café increase its profits?

clarifying_info.a: There are two other coffee shops in the nearby area that sell coffees and pastries. No further information is available on these competitors.
The café currently serves two items — coffee and latte — in three different sizes.

exhibits.title: Products, Costs and Customer Split
exhibits.shows: A table listing the two products (coffee and latte) across three sizes (small, medium, large), with price, cost, and the percentage of customers who order each size/product combination.
exhibits.data: Prices, costs per drink by size, and customer order mix percentages for coffee and latte across three sizes

exhibits.title: Demand of Coffee Per Hour
exhibits.shows: A table or chart showing the number of customers arriving at the café each hour from 7 AM to 10 PM, Monday through Friday.
exhibits.data: Customer count per hour for each hour of operation (7 AM–10 PM, Mon–Fri)

framework: External factors — Market: market growth trends, changing consumer preferences (product, atmosphere)
External factors — Competition: new low-cost competitors, new substitutes (restaurants or fast-food chains nearby)
Internal factors — Company: foot traffic / number of customers, process efficiency (average time per customer), capacity of the café
Internal factors — Product: limited product diversification, price sensitivity of customers, complementary products and services (e.g., wireless), quality and brand image

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the average profit per customer. Assume each customer purchases only one drink per visit.
questions.guidance: Strong candidates will calculate weighted average profit across all drink sizes and types using the customer mix percentages. They should note that larger sizes yield higher profit margins and suggest strategies like promoting larger sizes, introducing a 20 oz size, or eliminating 8 oz sizes. Profit here excludes barista labor costs.

math.setup: Weighted average profit = sum over all products of (price − cost) × customer mix %. Average Profitability = $1.50 per customer.
steps: For each size and product, compute margin = price − cost
Multiply each margin by the proportion of customers who order that item
Sum all weighted margins to get average profit per customer

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2 and the following information, calculate the average profit Marie's Café earns per day. Each customer purchases exactly one beverage. Two baristas work at any given time, paid $15/hour. Hours are 7 AM to 10 PM, Monday through Friday (closed weekends). Customers leave if they cannot be served quickly. On average it takes 2 minutes for a barista to complete an order.
questions.guidance: Candidate should determine the café's throughput capacity per hour (with 2 baristas at 2 min/order = 30 orders/barista/hour = 60 orders/hour capacity), compare capacity to actual hourly demand from Exhibit 2, calculate revenue-side profit using $1.50/customer (from Q1), deduct barista labor ($15/hour × 2 baristas = $30/hour), and sum across all hours. Candidate should identify that the café loses money in low-demand evening hours (barista cost exceeds profit contribution). Suggesting dynamic staffing — adding a third barista during morning peak and reducing to one barista in slow evening hours — improves daily profit from $607.50 to $787.50.

math.setup: Throughput capacity = 2 baristas × (60 min / 2 min per order) = 60 customers/hour. Hourly profit = min(actual demand, capacity) × $1.50 − 2 × $15. Sum across all 15 hours (7 AM–10 PM).
steps: Calculate maximum throughput per hour: 2 baristas × 30 orders/hour = 60 customers/hour
For each hour, served customers = min(demand from Exhibit 2, 60)
Sum all 15 hourly nets for daily profit
Optimized staffing (3 baristas in morning peak, 1 in slow evening hours): daily profit ≈ $787.50
math.answer: $607.50/day with 2 baristas throughout; $787.50/day with optimized staffing

questions.prompt: A new espresso machine priced at $2,000 can decrease the time it takes to make a latte. Average order completion time decreases from 2 minutes to 90 seconds. How long would it take to pay back the machine?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recalculate daily profit with the faster machine (90-second order time increases throughput to 40 orders/barista/hour = 80 orders/hour capacity with 2 baristas). With optimal staffing, the new daily profit is $922.50. Payback period = machine cost / incremental daily profit = $2,000 / ($922.50 − $787.50).

math.setup: New throughput = 2 baristas × (60 min / 1.5 min) = 80 customers/hour. Recalculate daily profit under optimal staffing. Payback = $2,000 / (new daily profit − old optimal daily profit).
steps: Recalculate daily profit with optimal staffing and new capacity: $922.50

brainstorming.prompt: Marie's Café does not offer wireless access for its customers. Should the café add this service?

categories.name: Positives
ideas: Attract more customers who want to work or browse while drinking coffee
Potential to charge customers for the wireless service
Customers may order larger sizes or stay longer, increasing spend per visit

categories.name: Negatives
ideas: Upfront cost of wireless setup and additional power outlets
May not have sufficient room for customers if they linger
Customers staying longer slows table turnover and reduces sales during busy periods
Could change the café's image and intimate atmosphere, alienating loyal customers

brainstorming.prompt: A competitor sells pastries, while Marie's Café does not. What factors should Marie's Café consider before purchasing an oven to sell pastries?

categories.name: Revenue
ideas: Pastry/doughnut sales revenue
Increased customer volume attracted by food offering
Synergies with coffee — customers more likely to buy both

categories.name: Fixed Costs
ideas: Purchasing and maintaining the oven
Setting up a display case
Storage space
Advertising the new offering

categories.name: Variable Costs
ideas: Ingredients for pastries
Hiring and training additional staff

categories.name: Capacity
ideas: Physical space in the café for an oven and ingredients
Whether existing baristas can accommodate increased demand

categories.name: Strategic Considerations
ideas: Brand Image — Marie's is known for coffee and atmosphere; adding pastries may dilute or change brand perception, especially if quality is low
Competition — need to assess price and quality versus competitors selling pastries
Alternative Opportunities — could source pastries from a third-party supplier rather than baking in-house

recommendation: Focus on driving profits through promoting larger drink sizes, which carry higher profit margins
Hire 4 baristas during peak morning hours and reduce to 2 baristas during slow periods to optimize labor costs
Offer complimentary add-on services such as wireless access to attract more customers
Diversify the product range by adding food items (e.g., sourcing pastries from a third party while capacity is limited)
risks: Offering wireless services may cause customers to stay longer, reducing table turnover and limiting capacity during peak hours
Baristas may be unable to accommodate a surge in demand if food is added without additional staffing
Adding pastries in-house requires capital investment and could affect brand image if quality is inconsistent
next_steps: Hire 4 baristas for peak hours or invest in the new espresso machine ($2,000, ~15-day payback) to increase throughput
Pilot food/pastry sales by sourcing from a third party first, before committing to an oven purchase
